report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that influenza vaccination causes Alzheimer’s disease is not supported by reliable evidence.

The strongest directly relevant evidence points in the opposite direction, but does **not** prove that flu vaccination prevents Alzheimer’s. A large U.S. claims-based cohort study found influenza vaccination was *associated* with a lower subsequent incidence of Alzheimer’s disease in adults 65 and older. Because it was observational, differences between people who do and do not vaccinate—health status, healthcare use, socioeconomic factors, and lifestyle—could partly explain the association; it cannot establish causation.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9484126/

Systematic reviews/meta-analyses of observational studies similarly report lower dementia risk among vaccinated older adults, while appropriately calling for more research to clarify mechanisms and causality. These findings are evidence *against* the proposed harmful effect, not proof of a cognitive benefit.  
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.3233/JAD-221036

I found no credible cohort study, randomized trial, systematic review, or established vaccine-safety finding showing increased Alzheimer’s incidence after influenza vaccination. Safety surveillance does recognize that vaccines can have rare adverse events; for flu vaccines, the best-established neurologic concern is a small, season-variable possible excess risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (about 1–2 additional cases per million doses), which is distinct from Alzheimer’s disease.  
https://www.cdc.gov/flu/vaccine-safety/guillainbarre.html

Alzheimer’s is a progressive disease with multifactorial causes and risk factors, rather than a known vaccine adverse effect.  
https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/alzheimers-causes-and-risk-factors/what-causes-alzheimers-disease
